title: Staff songwriter at Paramount and Hollywood's slow pace
summary: On staff pay of about a thousand a week he disliked Hollywood's slow tempo, since he needs each piece resolved.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You were on staff as to sit in the office and think of tunes, sort of assignment?

Right. They'd come running in and say, listen, there's a scene in the picture where Brian Donlevy's Donnelly has just killed a guy, as he's blowing the smoke out of his gun he's humming this cowboy song; write it. That was the assignment.
You were in pretty high cotton then weren't you, that was a lot of money compared to a band player?

Yes. My salary went up quite a bit, we were bringing in, at best, a couple of hundred, at least a thousand a week to begin with, and then they got more and more popular, people wanted my work and my income even raised above that. I was doing very well.
But the Hollywood experience wasn't an enjoyable one.
In what way?

Tempo. The tempo out there was very slow, too slow for me, so I had a piece of material that I wanted to sell and I was in New York, I'd go up to a publisher and I'd say, here's a thing I just wrote, and he'd say play it. I'd play and he'd say I want it, Sarah, bring in the contracts. I'd sign, my advance check and that's it. Or no, I don't like it, or it's nice but I can't use it; I had my answer then.

In Hollywood it was different. I'd go to the publisher, I'd say I have a song, he'd say great, I'll tell you what, this is January 10, meet me on the golf course July 15 at three o'clock and we'll kick it around.
Are you exaggerating?
Very slightly. Very slightly. He might have said June 15 instead of July, but that's the way it was and I couldn't

adjust to it.
I was making good money but I didn't feel that secure so that I could wait that period of time to find out what would happen. That slowed down everything.

For my own satisfaction I want to know what's going to happen with each thing I write, I cannot write and put it aside and get to the next thing and put it aside and get--I have to find out what's going to happen with each piece of work I do. It had to resolve itself. It has to be used, accepted, rejected, but it has to have a completion.
Sequel
Did Siegel react the same way to Hollywood?

No, he didn't react the same way. He was familiar with it. He had been out there before, not with the open door that he had this time, but he was used to that kind of tempo, he could adjust to it. I couldn't.
When you were on staff at a grand a week or something like that,
you were considered royalty, I presume, and were suddenly a very important man around town?
Yeah, people were coming to me with all kinds of things. I didn't feel like anything had changed, I felt like the same person.
Were you asked to do anything besides write songs? You weren't asked to do scoring?
The studio had no idea that I could write.
